Conditions have been challenging for the US solar industry over the past couple of years, as Washington’s energy priorities have shifted dramatically. Yet the industry has remained resilient, thanks in part to rapid growth in demand for electricity to power data centres. The key question for solar suppliers now is not how far they can cut greenhouse gas emissions, but how fast they can bring new generation capacity on line.
In this special episode from the RE+ conference in Las Vegas, Ed Crooks is joined by two leaders in US solar to discuss their perspectives on the changing outlook for the industry. Karen Bazela is the senior vice president of sales at Shoals Technologies Group, and Jessica Lawrence-Vaca is the chief commercial officer at Array Technologies. The two companies have announced a merger, with the aim of creating an integrated supplier for the solar and storage industries, including electrical balance of system solutions and trackers.
Karen and Jessica discuss speed to power as a central advantage of solar. With long lead times for other generation technologies such as gas turbines, solar can help meet near-term demand while other sources come online.
Policy whiplash has created challenges for the solar industry, but Karen and Jessica argue that it should be possible to get past some of the partisan division that has characterized the political debate over energy in recent years. They argue that policymakers should take an all-of-the-above approach, and reform permitting to expedite investment.
Jessica says the solar industry also needs to do a better job of advocating for itself. She argue that it needs to make a stronger case around American manufacturing, construction jobs, steel and energy security, not only climate benefits.
The domestic supply chain offers shorter lead times and more responsive service, but it comes with trade-offs. Karen says Shoals manufactures in the US while still sourcing some components overseas. Jessica says Array makes 85 to 90 per cent of its components in the US and recently opened a $50 million Albuquerque facility. The guests say a fully domestic supply chain cannot be built overnight, and that policy needs to distinguish between components that make sense to produce in America and those that do not. They note that trackers qualify for the 45X manufacturing tax credit, while electrical balance-of-systems equipment does not.
Finally, Karen and Jessica discuss their positions as high-profile women in leadership roles in an industry that remains male-dominated. They argue that there is a need to recruit more women and show that they can have pathways into senior roles, and they talk about the work they are doing to highlight the opportunities that the industry has to offer.
For more on careers for women in renewable energy, resources are available from Women in Renewable Energy (https://womeninrenewableenergy.ca/ ) and Women of Renewable Industries and Sustainable Energy (https://wrisenergy.org/).
 
This episode of the Energy Gang is brought to you by Shoals Technologies, a leading provider of electrical balance of systems (EBOS) solutions for solar, energy storage, and data centers. 
As electricity demand surges, the race is on to deliver solar projects faster, smarter, and more reliably. In this episode, leaders from Shoals Technologies and Array Technologies explore how smarter power distribution, solar trackers, domestic manufacturing, and streamlined installation can reduce complexity, accelerate construction, and bring reliable power online faster.
